task: Write one sentence of your own using the word execrable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know execrable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The critic spared the airport hotel exactly one word on the comment card — execrable — and underlined it twice.
Shoddy work cuts corners and shows it; execrable lives several floors further down.
Dreadful is very bad indeed, but execrable is the final rung — badness that invites cursing, the review written in a hiss.

Abominable condemns on moral grounds as much as on quality — we call cruelty, betrayals, and inhuman conditions abominable. Execrable stays a judgment of quality: work, performances, food so wretchedly bad they feel like an insult. An abominable act outrages the conscience; an execrable film only ruins the evening.

Atrocious is the everyday exaggeration for anything shockingly bad — atrocious traffic, atrocious handwriting — reached for casually and forgotten by dinner. Execrable is rarer and hotter, a formal curse a reviewer chooses deliberately, and it lands with the weight of a verdict rather than a groan.

Judge Ferro had scored the county fair's pie contest for twenty years, and his scale was famously plain: good, fair, poor.
One year, a single entry drove him past his own vocabulary.
The crust was raw in the middle and scorched at the rim; the filling had been salted where sugar was meant; the slice slumped sideways as if it wished to leave the plate.
Ferro wrote one word on the card — execrable — then explained to the new judges that he had used it twice in twenty years, and never lightly.
No one was wronged, he was careful to add.
